cards.title: July flooding in Toronto caused almost $1 billion in insured damage
cards.claim: CatIQ estimated the July 15-16, 2024 Toronto flash flood caused over $940 million in insured damage, showing Toronto can generate very large water losses in a single event.

stat.what: insured damage, Toronto flash flood July 2024 (CatIQ)

cards.relevance: A single-event spike shows Toronto's low average water-claim frequency can be overturned by extreme rain.
cards.limit: No claim counts or basement/sewer-backup split given; event total, not per-policy rate.

cards.title: Toronto and GTA Flash Flood Anniversary Underscores Urgency of Severe Weather Preparedness
cards.claim: IBC's anniversary release describes nearly $1 billion in insured personal-property damage from the July 2024 Toronto-area flash flood.
cards.relevance: Confirms IBC's own rounded total, reinforcing that Toronto is exposed to severe water events.
cards.limit: Rainfall and claim counts not in the article; figure rounded versus $940M CatIQ.

cards.title: City of Toronto to almost double basement flooding subsidies starting May 1
cards.claim: Toronto raised its maximum basement-flooding subsidy to $6,650 after over 1,000 homes flooded in 2024, with about 14% of eligible owners having participated since 2007.

stat.what: share of eligible Toronto property owners who used the subsidy program since 2007; ~59,000 applications, ~$86M

cards.relevance: Shows Toronto has a long-running protection program but modest uptake, so it is not simply immune.
cards.limit: Does not give properties protected or loss outcomes; mitigation effect on claims is not quantified.

cards.title: Early summer storms in Ontario and Quebec cause $439 million in insured damage
cards.claim: Ottawa recorded 118 mm on Canada Day 2026, an all-time July daily record, with over 4,500 basement floods reported by local officials.

stat.what: Ottawa rainfall July 1, 2026; reported basement floods

cards.relevance: Ottawa's 0.095 book rate is exposed to a 2026 event that a pre-2026 view would understate.
cards.limit: No claim counts; basement floods are municipal reports, not insured claims.

cards.title: Ottawa flash flood losses push Ontario-Quebec storm estimate to $491 million
cards.claim: CatIQ's 90-day estimate rose to $491 million, with over 70% of incurred losses coming from Nepean and southwest Ottawa.

stat.what: share of incurred total from Nepean and SW Ottawa, 2026 storm (CatIQ)

cards.relevance: Shows Ottawa losses were geographically concentrated, so a citywide rate hides neighbourhood hotspots.
cards.limit: Event covers Ontario and Quebec; no exact residential dollar split; estimate may still change.

cards.title: Ottawa boosts flood grant funding after record Canada Day storm
cards.claim: Ottawa offers a $1,000 compassionate grant and is expanding its protective plumbing program for backwater valves after a storm that more than doubled the prior July 1 rainfall record.

stat.what: July 1, 2026 Ottawa rainfall vs previous July 1 record (1959)

cards.relevance: Documents municipal mitigation levers and how extreme the rainfall was relative to history.
cards.limit: News summary of council actions; program uptake and effectiveness not given.

cards.title: Alberta floods the costliest insured natural disaster in Canadian history
cards.claim: IBC reported insured losses from the June 2013 Alberta floods above $1.7 billion with well over 25,000 claims, making it then the costliest insured disaster in Canada.

stat.what: insured losses and claims, June 2013 Alberta floods (PCS-Canada)

cards.relevance: Calgary's low current rate follows a catastrophic 2013 event, so the low rate is not a sign of structural safety.
cards.limit: 2013 estimate in nominal dollars; no sewer-backup versus overland split; pre-dates later mitigation.

cards.title: Flood resiliency improvements since 2013
cards.claim: Calgary says $1 billion invested since 2013 protects 4,245 properties and cuts damage risk from a 2013-sized flood by about 70%.

stat.what: claimed reduction in damage risk from a 2013-sized flood (City of Calgary)

cards.relevance: Large river-flood mitigation helps explain Calgary's lower water exposure than Montreal.
cards.limit: City self-reported; covers river flood, not sewer backup, which drives most Home water claims.

cards.title: Calgary, Toronto 2013 floods started national conversation on the insurance protection gap
cards.claim: IBC said the 2013 Calgary and Toronto floods together cost insurers about $3.1 billion, and since 2013 there have been 35 flood events above $30 million each.

stat.what: claims paid for the 2013 Calgary and Toronto floods combined (IBC)

cards.relevance: Puts both Toronto and Calgary on record as large water-loss events, a direct counter to the idea they are safe.
cards.limit: Event-based national release; no city-level claims-per-policy rates.

cards.title: Programme de subvention pour dispositifs anti-refoulement (Ville de Québec)
cards.claim: Québec City funds up to $1,500 per building for backwater devices on older single-family, semi-detached and row houses connected to the sanitary sewer.

stat.what: maximum subsidy per building for backwater prevention devices

cards.relevance: A funded backflow-prevention program for pre-2015 housing is a plausible reason for Québec City's low 0.043 rate.
cards.limit: Eligibility rules only; no uptake or claims-impact data; excludes condos and multi-unit buildings.

cards.title: ICCA report: Water on the Rise - Protecting Canadian homes from the growing threat of flooding
cards.claim: Intact Centre home assessments found 85% of Ontario homes lacked a backup sump pump or power and basement repair averaged $43,000 in 2018.

stat.what: assessed Ontario homes with no backup sump pump or backup power

cards.relevance: Indicates Ontario homes carry unmitigated basement-flood vulnerability despite lower observed claim rates.
cards.limit: Small sample (~500 homes, 2017-18) across Ontario and Saskatchewan; not city-representative.

cards.title: Ontario's flood season exposes the limits of optional overland cover
cards.claim: A September 2, 2026 Toronto storm brought 100-110 mm in one afternoon, and sewer backup and overland cover remain optional, often sublimited endorsements.

stat.what: Toronto rainfall in one afternoon, September 2, 2026

cards.relevance: A second extreme Ontario rain event in 2026 undercuts treating Toronto and Ottawa as low-water-risk.
cards.limit: Toronto loss estimate still pending in the article; no uptake rate given.

cards.title: TMR residents want answers after multiple floods
cards.claim: Residents of a Montreal-area suburb report repeat sewage basement floods costing about $80,000 each, and the municipality admitted it had not found anyone to clean sewers in two years.

stat.what: reported repair cost per basement flood, one TMR household

cards.relevance: Illustrates the local sewer-capacity and maintenance failures that distinguish Montréal from peer cities.
cards.limit: Single anecdotal household in a suburb; not representative of the city rate.
